items.label: f04-permission-vs-scope
items.front: Permission check vs data scope: what question does each answer?
items.back: Permission (canPerformAction): may this role do the action at all, e.g. grade? Scope (buildStudentScope): whose data, e.g. which students' work? A Teacher may grade, but only students in sections they teach.

items.label: f02-claim-is-the-count
items.front: How do you claim a queue row safely with Prisma?
items.back: updateMany({ where: { id, status: { in: RUNNABLE } }, data: { status: 'Running', attempts: { increment: 1 } } }) and treat count === 1 as the claim. The guard must be part of the write condition, not a prior SELECT.

items.label: f01-admin-fallback-fail-open
items.front: getActiveUser falls back to the 'admin' user when the cookie is missing or points at a deleted user. Risk?
items.back: Fail-open authentication: no session means full admin rights. Acceptable only for this lab's dev switcher; a real deployment must reject the request (401) instead.

items.label: f03-green-build-not-running-app
items.front: The repo shipped a 15-table dev.db against a 17-table schema and tsc, next build and 129 tests all passed. Lessons?
items.back: A generated artefact in version control is a liability (dev.db is now gitignored and rebuilt by db:push + db:seed), and a green build is not a running application: start the process, because only that read the real database.

items.prompt: Why does buildStudentScope return a Prisma WHERE fragment instead of filtering fetched students in JavaScript?

choices.text: A post-fetch filter breaks once someone adds take, count or an aggregate over unfiltered rows
JavaScript filters run on the client and cannot read the session cookie that identifies the viewer
WHERE fragments are cached by Next.js between requests, so pages render faster
Prisma cannot return students whose relations have not been loaded, so filtering in JavaScript would crash

JavaScript filters run on the client and cannot read the session cookie that identifies the viewer
WHERE fragments are cached by Next.js between requests, so pages render faster

items.explanation: Pushing the constraint into the query means it cannot be forgotten downstream; the scope module explains the 'silently too high' total leak of filtering after fetching.

items.prompt: Two workers try to run the same Queued job at once. Why does claimJob use updateMany with a status filter instead of reading the row and then calling update?

choices.text: The status check lives in the write's WHERE, so the database picks one winner (count 1 vs 0)
updateMany is faster than update on SQLite, so the window between the two workers becomes too small to matter
update cannot increment a column atomically, so the attempts counter could not be maintained with it
updateMany locks the whole table until the job finishes running

choices: The status check lives in the write's WHERE, so the database picks one winner (count 1 vs 0)
updateMany is faster than update on SQLite, so the window between the two workers becomes too small to matter
update cannot increment a column atomically, so the attempts counter could not be maintained with it
updateMany locks the whole table until the job finishes running

items.explanation: SELECT-then-UPDATE lets both workers see Queued and both execute. updateMany({ where: { id, status: { in: RUNNABLE } } }) returns a count, and only one call can match.
